utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is Case Number IT-00-39 and 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Mark Harmon, and Fergal Gaynor appearing for the Prosecution, with Carmela Annink-javier assisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Deyan Brashich for the Krajisnik Defence. I am joined by Mr. Nikola Kostich and I would like to apprise the Court that Mr. Trivan Vovicic, a representative of Republika Srpska here in The Hague is sitting because of circumstances at the Defence table. And I'm sure he will introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would like to introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VOVICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Trivan Vovicic. I'm a representative of the government of Republika Srpska, and I'm the liaison officer for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the hearing of an application for provisional release on behalf of the accused Momcilo Krajisnik. We have received pleadings on behalf of both the applicant and the respondent. There's no need for anyone to repeat those, but we'll hear oral argument. We would be grateful if the parties were brief, and at the end, we'll hear from the representative of the Republika Srpska. Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appear once again before this Chamber requesting a provisional release on behalf of my client, Mr. Krajisnik. The Krajisnik Defence is mindful that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal does not allow for motions for reconsideration. However, Your Honour, I think that a change in circumstance has occurred, and a significant change in circumstance which would warrant the granting of the relief. The accused has sought provisional release either in the Republika Srpska or, in the alternative, in the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslavia. And I will just say Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, because the union between Serbia and Montenegro appears to be in some state of flux. However, the Republic of Serbia has passed a law on cooperation with the Tribunal. I am mindful of the decision rendered by this Chamber in another case recently, but that case somewhat is not in point. The real case in point is the case of the accused Cesic. Cesic is a Bosnian Serb. He was on the territory of the Republic of Serbia. He was arrested by the authorities of the Republic of Serbia, and delivered through legal mechanisms to the custody of The Hague. We have at this present time a precedent that a Bosnian Serb found on the territory of the Republic of Serbia will be dealt with in accordance with those promises and representations that had been made to the international community. Mr. Krajisnik is a Bosnian Serb. Should this Court allow him provisional release on the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and should he not adhere to the terms and conditions imposed by this Chamber, he will be promptly arrested, dealt with, and brought back to The Hague. One of the indices, at least in my national jurisdiction, of someone to be released on bail is, of course, ties to the community. With regard to ties to the community, Mr. Krajisnik's brother lives in Belgrade and would give him a place where to reside while awaiting trial. I will not speak for Mr. Vovicic. I will let him address the Court himself on behalf of the Republika Srpska. But I have been given to understand and I warrant and make a representation that all of the guarantees and representations that were made six months ago on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik, should the Chamber allow the alternative place of provisional release, that is, the Republika Srpska and Pale, are still in place. All that I have said before, including my own representations on behalf of my client, I am willing to repeat, but I don't think that the Court has to hear my broken record. Mr. Krajisnik, I spoke to him yesterday, assures me again that he will make any and all representations, warranties, promises to this Tribunal, to well and faithfully obey the orders and conditions and is prepared to make such a representation orally. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, what would you say is the new circumstance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Two, things, Your Honour. If we send Mr. Krajisnik to the Republic of Serbia, we have, one, a law that has been passed for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cooperation with The Hague which did not occur -- or which was not in place when the last application was made. And the second changed circumstance is a specific showing by the authorities of the Republic of Serbia or Yugoslavia where they have arrested an accused Bosnian Serb on the territory of Yugoslavia, have gone through the legal process in the legislation being brought before a court of law, having the indictment read to the accused. I believe that the law provides for a very short window in which the accused can take certain acts vis-a-vis the -- vis-a-vis the indictment, then thereafter he is extradited and delivered on to the Tribunal. If you will bear with me, Judge Robinson, Mr. Kostich also reminds me that the changed circumstance again with regard to the Republic of Serbia and to Yugoslavia is the continued cooperation with regard to witnesses and documents showing the authorities in Serbia are moving towards full compliance with their obligations with regard to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I suppose this point has to be faced, that this accused has been in custody a long time as the Tribunal or the Trial Chamber acknowledges. But there is now the prospect of a trial in November. How realistic is an application which, provided the trial comes on then, is four months off?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Judge May, the Defence has been working day and night to prepare for trial. We are trying, and hopefully, the trial could start in November, but as things happen, it may be delayed. We have Mr. Krajisnik, who has been incarcerated since April of 2000. I know the case, I think, well, and I have a very strong belief that Mr. Krajisnik, a parliamentarian, will be vindicated and will be found not guilty by this Tribunal. Tat is his wish, and that is what we are striving for. And a vindication of his innocence of the charges will never bring back two and a half years, or two years and three months of his life as a normal, constructive human being that he was prior to the troubles in Bosnia. Even if we give him the freedom of three months or four months to be with his aged mother, if you'll recall one of the applications we had made was on the eve and then death of his father. His mother has been -- which I did not bring out in the moving papers. But I will warrant and make a representation that I have in my possession the reports, prognosis, and medical findings of the military hospital in Belgrade with regard to his mother, and that the prognosis is not favourable. Mr. Krajisnik, as was evidenced in the earlier application, is a deeply and -- and that was the letter of support by his holiness, the head of the Serbian orthodox church -- is again, as I said, he's a very religious man. Even if the trial starts in October, he will have had July, August, September with his mom. Yes, he will have to come back, and based on the position taken by the Dutch authorities, will go back in jail for a year, year and a half, two years when this trial will take place with 405 witnesses by the Prosecution, and 150 by the Krajisnik Defence, again, those years will never be returned to him. And he's prepared to do that, to vindicate his name. But we would have given him something which he will never be able to regain, and that is a couple of months with his mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will attempt to address only those issues raised by Mr. Brashich in his oral argument rather than revisit the discussions in the written submissions. Mr. Brashich raised two changes of circumstance: The first cited was the law on cooperation. However, his assessment that the status of the Federation appears to be in some state of flux is even something of an understatement. There is a reconfiguration in the offing, agreements have been signed by all the parties, and under those agreements, there would be no Federal Ministry of Interior, the operative body which would be called upon to oversee any guarantees it issued, and any cooperation which needed to be enlisted. Beyond that, even at present, it's the Republic of Serbia authorities who function in the operative role required here. It's the Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, which is called upon to execute arrest warrants, monitor people, to conduct the tasks necessary to ensure to the extent an entity is willing and able to do so that someone will appear for trial. That's why, in previous applications of this type, there has been a guarantee from the Republic of Serbia, or joint guarantees from the FRY and the Republic of Serbia. And there is no such guarantee here. Mr. Brashich also cited the instance of the arrest of a Bosnian Serb, Mr. Cesic. And I would urge the Court to note the distinction between Mr. Cesic's circumstances. He is a low-level perpetrator from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brcko area with other circumstances in which arrests have been required. For example, I believe that Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Radic from the Vukovar indictment, former military officials, have been residing in the Republic of Serbia for a long period time, a fact known to the Tribunal and to the authorities. The OTP has made repeated efforts to ensure their arrest. That the problems associated with that failure are clearly associated with the perceived status of those persons. I suggest respectfully that the calculations involved in determining whether resources will be committed and whether a political commitment will exist to arrest one person are not the same as in the case of another potentially more influential person. Beyond that, which addresses only the question of willingness, is the question of wherewithal. Mr. Krajisnik's closest colleagues, also persons of political or military influence and significance in Republika Srpska, have demonstrated considerable agility and success in evading the authorities and remaining out of custody, specifically by enlisting the sympathies and support of persons who continue to hold them in high regard. Another factor to be considered in the distinctions between the situation that Mr. Brashich has cited and the circumstances we must examine here. As a general matter, the jurisprudence of this institution reflect some consistency in those applications for provisional release which have been successful, and that has been particularly pronounced in the recent past, and that is the following: The accused voluntarily surrendered; the accused had a guarantee from the Republik to which he sought release; and there was a long period of time anticipated between the motion and the trial date. Just to add one additional point, Your Honour, while still attempting to remain brief, I noted Mr. Brashich's benign account of Mr. Krajisnik's -- rather glowing account of his character and his passive role in what Mr. Brashich called the troubles and the invocation of some emotional factors, and I would suggest that any kind of appeal to the emotions is not appropriate in light of the massive sufferings reflected in the indictment. And that's all I'll say in response to that aspect of his appeal. I urge the Court to focus on the totality of the circumstances, the circumstances have certainly not changed in a meaningful way to justify any departure from the previous rulings. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brashich, is there something you want to say in reply briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Three things, Your Honour. We have a guarantee from Yugoslavia. We have a guarantee from Srpska. If the Court wants to make a condition on the guarantee of the Republic of Serbia, I will certainly endeavour to try. Two, the two individuals who were mentioned who have not been arrested are military officers and that's Sljivancanin and Radic. And three, Your Honour, I still believe there's a presumption of innocence in the statute. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jovocic, is there anything you'd like to add to what has been said already?

utterances.speaker: MR. VOVICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to address you. First of all, may I say that the government of the Republika Srpska fully abides by the guarantees that have already been provided to you. By your leave, I should also like to say that Mr. Tieger, perhaps made an oversight. Mr. Krajisnik was not publicly indicted, and therefore he had no possibility of voluntarily surrendering. I can also confirm on behalf of the government of Republika Srpska, that if Mr. Krajisnik is provisionally released and if he goes to Republika Srpska, the government will fully abide by all the rulings of the Trial Chamber. Whenever the Trial Chamber allowed persons from the territory of Republika Srpska to be provisionally released, all these persons fully abided by the rulings of the Court and at the request of the Trial Chamber, they were all returned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovocic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I just wondered about the absence of a guarantee from the Republic of Serbia. And there was one that was produced in the previous hearing, but it strikes me that your application would be stronger if you had one for the current hearing. Because I always want to know whether that guarantee still holds in respect of the new application.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is my fault. That was my oversight, and perhaps not being as thorough as I should have been on behalf of my client. So I take the blame for that omission, and I will try and rectify that and file a guarantee from the present Republic of Serbia. And the only thing which I would add to that would be the assurances made in the Ojdanic case before this very Chamber, and rely on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the one, my completing the record, and two, seeking the Chamber to take judicial notice of the testimony in the Ojdanic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and I know you want to be brief. Just one quick point of clarification and another point. In response to Judge Robinson's questions, I'm not sure if there was a misunderstanding in the last exchange. I don't believe there was ever a guarantee from the Republic of Serbia. I think the guarantee that was presented before was from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which is part of the reason I focussed on the distinction earlier. And I'd finally note that with respect to Republika Srpska, that it is still the case that no publicly indicted person has been arrested by the Republika Srpska authorities, and in fact, the gentleman who was apprehended by SFOR yesterday I believe was publicly indicted and was arrested at his home. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will consider this matter, and we will give our decision in writing. We'll rise now. Reconvene shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.09, to be followed by an Ex Parte. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
